interactions.summary: Jiang closes the Piccarda thought experiment by saying that will itself creates an opening, even if he is not claiming any single tactic is guaranteed.
A student challenges Jiang with the case of good pagans, and Jiang answers that Dante departs from a simple church identity test because pagans can appear in heaven.

Another student worries that the soldiers might call Piccarda’s threat a bluff, but Jiang says no one would take that chance; even the duke’s pay structure still leaves the safer choice as retreat, which restates his thesis that real will finds a path.
A student reads the passage in which Piccarda vanishes singing Ave Maria and Dante turns back toward Beatrice with his question delayed by brightness.

claims.claim: Jiang says the larger lesson of the Piccarda scenario is that where there is real will, there is always some way through the situation even if the exact tactic is hypothetical.
Jiang says Dante does not share the simple Catholic rule that Christian identity alone determines heaven or hell, and he tells the class they will later find pagans in heaven.

Jiang argues that a soldier facing Piccarda on the roof would not risk calling her bluff, because the consequences of storming the nunnery and causing her death are worse than retreating and reporting failure.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces the whole scene to a brutal practical maxim: if you have the will, there is always going to be a way.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you have the will there's always going to be a way
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest reusable compression of the packet and of the broader Piccarda argument.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang bluntly breaks church identity from salvation by telling the class that Dante puts pagans in heaven.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there are pagans who are in heaven
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet’s sharpest doctrinal pressure point and opens later comparative reading of Dante against institutional Catholicism.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student’s test case for whether moral action without Christian belief can still receive heavenly reward in Dante.
A student’s phrase for the graded structure of heaven that Jiang has been mapping through the Piccarda discussion.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet joins Jiang’s will-centered reading of Piccarda to an explicit claim that Dante outruns a simple Christian-versus-pagan salvation divide.
